title: Unbounded knapsack
sub: Coin Change: why greedy breaks, dp[s] = min(dp[s − c] + 1), and how loop order tells combinations from permutations
cards/0/title: Coin Change: the problem and the first idea
cards/0/body:
Coin Change (LeetCode #322). Given coin denominations coins (up to 12 distinct ones) and an amount up to 10⁴, with an unlimited supply of every coin, find the minimum number of coins that make exactly amount, or −1 if it can’t be done.

The signals: the question asks for a minimum, not a list; every item can be taken without limit; the remainder after choosing a coin is the same problem with a smaller amount. This is the unbounded knapsack: fill a “capacity” with items that each come in an infinite supply.

The first thing that comes to mind is greedy: take the largest coin that still fits into the remainder until the remainder is zero. For ordinary money — 1, 2, 5, 10, 50 — this really does give the minimum. The question an interviewer asks: and for arbitrary denominations?
cards/1/q: coins = [1, 3, 4], amount = 6. How many coins does the greedy code from the previous card use, and what is the optimum?
cards/1/options/3: Greedy −1: after 4, the remainder 2 can’t be made
cards/1/explain: Greedy takes 4 and makes the remainder 2 out of ones: 4 + 1 + 1 — three coins. But 3 + 3 is two. The large coin is “good” only right now: it leaves a remainder that is expensive to fill. The decision at a step depends on everything after it — so you have to try the choices, not take one.
cards/1/wrong/1: There is no 2 among the denominations: 4 + 2 can’t be made.
cards/1/wrong/2: Greedy starts with the largest coin — 4, not 3. Only a search would find 3 + 3.
cards/1/wrong/3: The remainder 2 is made of two ones — there is a 1, so greedy doesn’t get stuck. It can get stuck on denominations without a one: [3, 5] and the sum 9 — after 5 the remainder is 4, after 3 it is 1, while 3 + 3 + 3 exists.
cards/2/title: dp[s]: the minimum for every sum
cards/2/body:
Greedy may not find an answer at all: on [3, 5] and the sum 9 it takes 5, then 3 — and gets stuck on the remainder 1, although 3 + 3 + 3 exists. So the coin has to be chosen not by one rule but by trying the options.

Trying every choice is the decision tree from the first lesson, and it is exponential. But the subproblem “the minimum coins for sum s” depends only on s, not on how we got there: the remainder 2 after a 4 and the remainder 2 after 1 + 3 are the same problem. There are only amount + 1 subproblems — that is DP.

State: dp[s] is the minimum number of coins for the sum s. Transition: the last coin was some c, and before it — the optimum for s − c: dp[s] = min over c ≤ s of dp[s − c] + 1. Base: dp[0] = 0. Order: s ascending — every s − c is smaller than s. Answer: dp[amount].

Unreachable sums. They need an “∞”. int.MaxValue is dangerous: + 1 overflows. Use amount + 1 — you never need more than amount coins (even all ones), so this number works as infinity, and + 1 is safe. If at the end dp[amount] > amount, the sum is unreachable and the answer is −1.

Cost: O(amount·k) time — with 10⁴ and 12 coins that is 1.2·10⁵ steps; O(amount) memory.
cards/2/flow/2: for every c ≤ s: dp[s − c] + 1
cards/3/explain: “∞” is amount + 1: int.MaxValue + 1 overflows. The base is zero coins for the zero sum. The transition is the last coin c, and before it the optimum for i − c; dp[i − 1] + 1 would mean “the last coin is always 1”. An unreachable sum is −1 by the problem statement.
cards/4/task: Walk the dp filling for coins = [1, 3, 4], amount = 6. The arcs are transitions from dp[s − c]. The rig will stop twice and ask what goes into a cell: compute from the table, not greedily.
cards/4/goal/asks/0/q: dp[1] = 1, dp[2] = 2. What goes into dp[3]?
cards/4/goal/asks/0/explain: Candidates: coin 1 — dp[2] + 1 = 3, coin 3 — dp[0] + 1 = 1. The minimum is 1: the sum 3 is one coin. Coin 4 is larger than the sum and isn’t considered. 3 is “all ones” — what you’d get looking only at dp[i − 1].
cards/4/goal/asks/1/q: dp[3] = 1, dp[4] = 1, dp[5] = 2. What goes into dp[6]?
cards/4/goal/asks/1/explain: Coin 1: dp[5] + 1 = 3. Coin 3: dp[3] + 1 = 2. Coin 4: dp[2] + 1 = 3. The minimum is 2, via the 3: 3 + 3. The greedy path 4 + 1 + 1 is the option through dp[2], and the table honestly counts it as three coins.
cards/5/q: Here “∞” is int.MaxValue. On coins = [2], amount = 3 the code returned −2147483648. Tap the line where that number came from.
cards/5/explain: dp[1] is unreachable and stays int.MaxValue. For i = 3, coin 2 gives dp[1] + 1 — an overflow in C#’s unchecked arithmetic: int.MaxValue + 1 = int.MinValue, and Math.Min happily picks it. The cure is “∞” = amount + 1, or checking dp[i − c] != int.MaxValue before the + 1.
cards/6/title: Which coins, BFS, and where this shows up in games
cards/6/body:
Recovering the set. Next to dp keep last[s] — the coin on which the minimum was reached. The answer is assembled from the end: s → s − last[s] until you reach zero. This is the standard trick for any DP: remember which transition won and walk those transitions back.

The same answer by breadth-first search. The sums 0…amount are vertices, a coin is an edge “+c”. The minimum number of coins is the shortest path from 0 to amount in an unweighted graph, and breadth-first search gives exactly that: a queue of sums, each visited once. The complexity is the same, O(amount·k), but BFS stops as soon as it reaches amount — earlier on “lucky” inputs.

In a game. Crafting from fixed-size resource bundles (bundles of 1, 3, 4 — make exactly 6 with the fewest bundles), giving change in an in-game currency with unusual denominations, picking a set of rewards worth exactly N points. A game designer sets the denominations — and nobody promises that greedy is correct for them. A table of 10⁴ cells is 40 KB and a fraction of a millisecond: it can be recomputed when the config changes and kept ready.
cards/7/title: The number of ways: loop order decides
cards/7/body:
Coin Change II (LeetCode #518): how many sets of coins make amount? Sets ignore order: 1 + 2 and 2 + 1 are one. The transition is “sum instead of minimum”: dp[s] += dp[s − c], with the base dp[0] = 1 — one way to make zero: take nothing.

But now the loop order matters. If coins are outside and sums inside — after processing coins coins[0..j], dp[s] holds the number of sets made of those coins only. Every set is built in one order — “all ones first, then all twos” — and counted once. That is the answer to #518.

If sums are outside and coins inside, then dp[s] = Σ dp[s − c] tries the last coin for every sum — and counts sequences: 1 + 2 and 2 + 1 separately. That is a different problem, Combination Sum IV (#377). For coins = [1, 2] and amount = 3 there are 2 sets and 3 sequences.

For the minimum the order doesn’t matter: the minimum over sets and over sequences is the same.

Each coin once (the 0/1 knapsack, Partition Equal Subset Sum, #416): coins outside, and sums inside descending. Then dp[s − c] hasn’t seen coin c yet, and it can’t be taken twice. Ascending — as in #518 — the same number can be taken again. Time O(n·W), where W is the capacity.
cards/8/q: In Change the loops were swapped: s from 1 to amount outside, foreach over coins inside. What does the code return on coins = [1, 2], amount = 4?
cards/8/options/0: 5 — the number of sequences, not sets
cards/8/options/1: 3 — the same as before: loop order doesn’t matter
cards/8/options/2: 4 — every coin is counted once extra
cards/8/options/3: 2 — every coin is taken at most once
cards/8/explain: With sums outside, for every sum we try the last coin: dp = 1, 1, 2, 3, 5. Those are all ordered decompositions: 1+1+1+1, 1+1+2, 1+2+1, 2+1+1, 2+2. Only three of them are distinct sets — {1,1,1,1}, {1,1,2}, {2,2} — and that is what the coins-outside version counts.
cards/8/wrong/1: 3 is what the original code with coins outside returns. With the loops swapped, 1 + 2 and 2 + 1 are counted separately.
cards/8/wrong/2: There is no extra one per coin: the difference is not a constant but what is being counted — sets or sequences.
cards/8/wrong/3: “At most once” is the 0/1 knapsack: coins outside and sums descending. Here the sums go up, and repeats are allowed.
cards/9/q: What is true about the problems in this lesson? Select all.
cards/9/options/0: For the minimum number of coins, the “coins/sums” loop order doesn’t change the answer
cards/9/options/1: If the denominations are 1, 2, 5, 10, 50, greedy gives the minimum and DP isn’t needed
cards/9/options/2: “∞” = amount + 1 is safe: dp[s − c] + 1 doesn’t overflow, and you never need more than amount coins
cards/9/options/3: The greedy algorithm always finds some decomposition if one exists
cards/9/options/4: In the 0/1 knapsack the inner loop over capacity goes downward
cards/9/explain: The minimum over sets and over sequences is the same — loop order only matters for counting ways. For “nice” denominations like ordinary money greedy is optimal, but not for arbitrary ones, and in an interview the denominations are almost always arbitrary. amount + 1 is an honest infinity. Greedy can get stuck: [3, 5], the sum 9. The descending loop in the 0/1 knapsack keeps an item from being taken twice.
cards/10/q: You are solving Coin Change out loud. Put the steps of the explanation in order.
cards/10/items/0: Clarify: unlimited coins? what to return if impossible? what are amount and the number of denominations?
cards/10/items/1: Suggest greedy and immediately a counterexample: [1, 3, 4] and 6 — 4 + 1 + 1 versus 3 + 3
cards/10/items/2: The state dp[s] and the transition: min over coins of dp[s − c] + 1
cards/10/items/3: Base dp[0] = 0, “∞” = amount + 1, order — s ascending
cards/10/items/6: Edge cases: amount = 0, an unreachable sum — −1
cards/10/explain: Greedy with a counterexample is a strong move: you show yourself why DP is needed before the interviewer asks. Then the five DP questions, a run over the table and the cost. amount = 0 is a common trap: the answer is 0, not −1.
cards/11/body:
Coin Change is the model of a whole family: “fill a capacity with items” (the knapsack). Minimum, maximum, number of ways or “is it possible” — only the operation in the transition changes: min, max, +, ||. A limit on how many of each item you may take changes the direction of the inner loop.

To “what if amount is up to 10⁹?” the answer is that the table won’t do: O(amount·k) depends on the magnitude of the number, not on the input size. Then you look for something else: the math of the denominations, BFS with pruning, limits on the number of coins.
cards/11/deep:
Correctness. Optimal substructure: if an optimal set for s contains coin c, the remaining coins are an optimal set for s − c. Otherwise we would replace them with a better set for s − c and get fewer coins for s than the “optimum”. So the minimum over the last coin covers every optimal candidate.

When greedy is correct. Coin systems for which greedy always gives the minimum are called canonical; ordinary coins and notes are like that. A system can be checked: if it contains a 1 and greedy is ever wrong, the smallest counterexample is below the sum of the two largest denominations — comparing greedy with DP on the sums up to that bound is enough. In an interview “not for arbitrary denominations, here is a counterexample” is enough.

Pseudo-polynomial time. O(amount·k) is polynomial in the value of amount, but a 30-bit number can be 10⁹: in terms of input length that is exponential. That is why the general knapsack stays a hard problem, and DP over capacity only works when the capacity is small. If the capacity is huge but there are only 20–40 items — enumerate subsets, or “meet in the middle” (enumerate each half of the items, then sort and binary search): O(2^(n/2)·n).

Top-down. A memoized recursion over s goes as deep as amount — 10⁴ frames with a coin of 1. That still fits in the stack (the first unit: thousands and tens of thousands of calls are fine), but the margin is small, and with amount 10⁶ the recursion would crash — one more reason to write the table.

.NET and Unity. int[amount + 1] for 10⁴ is 40 KB: allocate once and reuse it if you compute often. For small sums in hot code — Span<int> dp = stackalloc int[amount + 1] (keep amount small: a thread stack is on the order of a megabyte). Code with no reference types inside the loop maps well to a Burst job over a NativeArray<int>.
cards/12/q: Match the problem with how its loops are arranged.
